questions.question: An integer n is B-smooth if:
options: Every prime factor of n is ≤ B, letting n factor over the small-prime base
n is divisible by every prime up to B, regardless of multiplicities involved
n has exactly B prime factors when counted with multiplicity (Ω(n) = B)
n ≡ 0 (mod B!) — equivalent to having every small prime as a factor once
questions.explanation: B-smooth: all prime factors ≤ B. Density Ψ(x, B) is the Dickman function.

questions.question: What is the Hidden Subgroup Problem (HSP)?
options: Given f: G → S constant on cosets of an unknown H ≤ G, find a generating set of H
Given a subgroup H of G, list all of its non-trivial cosets and their representatives
Given a function f on G, decide whether f has any periodic structure at all
Given a permutation of G, find its order via repeated composition with itself
questions.explanation: HSP: f hides H by being constant on each coset and distinct between cosets. Find H. Many crypto problems reduce here (factoring, DLP, hidden shift).

questions.question: Why does Shor's quantum algorithm factor `n` in polynomial time?
options: It solves HSP on Z (period finding for f(x) = a^x mod n) via quantum Fourier transform
It runs Pollard-rho on a quantum computer with O(√p) qubit parallelism per iteration
It applies Grover's search over divisors d ≤ √n in O(n^(1/4)) quantum queries
It uses Quantum Index Calculus directly on the multiplicative group (Z/nZ)*
questions.explanation: Shor reduces factoring to finding the period r of f(x) = a^x mod n. Quantum period-finding (HSP on Z) is poly-time via QFT.

questions.question: What is the smooth-number density Ψ(x, x^(1/u)) asymptotically?
options: ρ(u)·x where ρ is the Dickman function — most integers near x are NOT u-smooth
x / log u — logarithmic decay, mild smoothness loss as u grows beyond 2
x^(1 − 1/u) — polynomial decay, used in Pollard-rho complexity analysis
exp(−u) · x — exponential decay, justifying the L-notation for sieves
questions.explanation: Ψ(x, x^(1/u)) ~ ρ(u)·x where ρ(u) is the Dickman function. ρ(2) ≈ 0.307, ρ(3) ≈ 0.049, ρ(5) ≈ 0.0035 — drops fast.

questions.question: Why are smooth numbers central to sub-exponential factoring (QS, NFS)?
options: Smooth values factor over a fixed small-prime base, enabling F₂ linear algebra to find squares
Smooth values are prime themselves, providing direct factors of n upon discovery
Smooth values increase the probability that Pollard-rho cycles converge quickly
Smooth values make modular exponentiation cheaper via the Pohlig-Hellman trick
questions.explanation: Sieve relations only when Q-values are B-smooth → factor over the prime base. The trade-off (small B → few relations smooth; large B → many primes to track) gives the L[1/2] / L[1/3] complexity.

questions.question: Which problems reduce to HSP on abelian groups (solvable by Shor-style quantum algorithm)?
options: Factoring integers, DLP in (Z/pZ)*, and DLP on elliptic curves all reduce to abelian HSP
Factoring and DLP do; lattice problems like SVP reduce to non-abelian HSP only
Only DLP in finite fields reduces; factoring reduces to a distinct quantum routine
Only DLP on elliptic curves reduces; factoring and (Z/pZ)*-DLP are unaffected
questions.explanation: Factoring ↔ Period finding on Z. DLP (any group) ↔ HSP on Z×Z. EC-DLP same. All abelian HSP, all poly-time on quantum. Lattice problems reduce to dihedral HSP — believed quantum-hard.

questions.question: Optimal smoothness bound B for QS is approximately:
options: B = exp(½ · √(ln n · ln ln n)) — balancing sieve cost against linear-algebra cost
B = √n — half the bit length of n for efficient trial-divide sieving above this
B = log² n — keeps the factor base polynomial in the input size of n
B = (log n)^3 — matches the size of the linear system Gaussian elimination handles
questions.explanation: Optimal B = L_n[1/2, 1/2]. Balances expected number of smooth relations with sieve interval and matrix size. Gives QS its L_n[1/2, 1] runtime.

questions.question: Post-quantum schemes (Kyber, Dilithium) resist Shor because their hard problems:
options: Reduce to non-abelian HSP (dihedral) or lattice problems with no known abelian-HSP form
Use quantum-resistant primes p ≡ 1 (mod 2^256) that defeat Shor's period finding
Replace integer arithmetic with floating-point operations, breaking unitarity assumptions
Encode messages in entangled qubit states that defeat measurement-based attacks
questions.explanation: Lattice / code / hash problems: no known reduction to abelian HSP. Dihedral HSP gives a quantum sub-exponential attack on lattices, but parameters are chosen well beyond that threshold.
